title: How Many Unplugged Wells Remain? | CAPIT Data Context
description: What national counts of abandoned, orphaned, and idle oil and gas wells actually measure, with the latest estimates and their sources.
headline: How Many Unplugged Wells Remain?
body: It depends on what you count. National figures range from about 142,000 documented orphan wells to more than 2 million unplugged abandoned wells, and each number measures something different. The most-quoted figure, roughly 3.7 million "abandoned wells," includes wells that have already been plugged.

sections.heading: The Numbers, and What Each One Counts
sections.body: The four figures you'll see most often:
bullets: **About 3.7 million abandoned wells** (EPA greenhouse gas inventory, 2021 data): every non-producing oil and gas well EPA estimates exists, plugged or not. EPA estimated about 58%, roughly 2.1 million, were unplugged. EPA lacks records for many pre-1975 wells and assumes those are unplugged.
**141,959 documented orphan wells** (Interstate Oil and Gas Compact Commission, as of December 31, 2023): wells in 29 state inventories with no responsible operator, up 54% since 2020.
**250,000 to 740,000 undocumented orphan wells** (IOGCC estimate): wells believed to exist but missing from state records or lacking precise locations.

**More than 11,400 orphan wells plugged with federal infrastructure funds** (U.S. Department of the Interior, through January 31, 2026): progress under the $4.7 billion orphan well program created by the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.

sections.heading: Idle and Inactive Wells
sections.body: There is no reliable national count of idle or inactive wells. States define idle status differently: Texas applies its inactive-well rules after 12 months without activity, California defines an idle well at 24 months, and federal law uses 4 years.

sections.heading: Key Terms
sections.body: These words are used differently from agency to agency:
bullets: **Orphan (or orphaned) well:** a well with no operator who can be found or who is able to plug it. For wells on state and private land, federal law defers to each state's definition.
**Idle or inactive well:** a well that isn't producing but usually still has an operator responsible for it.
**Temporarily abandoned or shut-in well:** a non-producing well the operator has permission to keep for possible future use, usually with periodic testing.
**Abandoned well:** used inconsistently. EPA counts plugged and unplugged wells; some states use the term only for unplugged wells, others only for plugged ones.

**Documented vs. undocumented:** a documented well has a regulatory record establishing that it exists, including its precise location. An undocumented well is unknown to regulators or still needs its location verified.

sections.heading: Why Transparent Tracking Matters
sections.body: Well information is spread across dozens of state agencies, federal programs, and private efforts, and a single state may publish only part of its inventory. That makes national progress hard to measure. CAPIT brings plugged-well records from state sources into one public view, labels what each figure counts, and keeps each record's source and revision history visible, so the public, landowners, and policymakers can see what has been done and how much work remains.
